claims.text: The nanoparticles are equimolar Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloys.
The nanoparticles are maintained within a 5–50 nm size range.
The nanoparticles are homogeneously chemically mixed.
Premelting and melting are governed by a statistical distribution of localized activation-energy barriers for atomic diffusion.
Chemical complexity generates the distribution of localized diffusion barriers.
Surface and interior regions begin atomic rearrangement and melting at different temperatures.
Differences among local atomic environments produce a spread of diffusion-energy barriers.
Regions with lower activation-energy barriers undergo premelting rearrangements first as temperature increases.
Sequential rearrangement of regions with different barriers produces multiple localized melting events rather than one sharp transition.
The melting curve will be broadened or contain multiple endothermic shoulders.
Endothermic shoulders will correlate with sequential localized melting events.
Systems with a narrow distribution of activation energies are expected to melt more uniformly.
The proposed baseline has a single broad melting peak without resolved sub-transitions.
The mechanism is proposed to apply to equimolar Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles between 5 and 50 nm under inert heating conditions.
The mechanism may not apply to non-equimolar compositions.
Significant surface modification may alter the energy landscape and invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Heating is to be conducted from room temperature to above complete melting at 1–10 °C/min in an inert atmosphere.
Molecular-dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations can provide activation-energy distributions for comparison with localized melting onsets.
